name: Health Insurance (US Payers)
one_liner: US health insurers collect premiums from employers, individuals and government programs and pay medical claims, earning thin margins on large volumes through managed care.
how_it_makes_money: Payers earn premiums for fully insured members and administrative fees for self-insured employer plans, then manage medical costs through provider networks, negotiated rates, utilization management and care management. Many are vertically integrated with PBMs, which earn from drug-plan administration, rebate retention and spread, and mail-order and specialty pharmacy.
value_chain: Employers, government and individuals buy coverage
revenue_formula: Underwriting margin = premiums - medical costs (medical loss ratio) - administrative costs
PBM revenue = prescriptions × (spread + admin fee) + retained rebates + specialty pharmacy sales
cost_structure: Medical claims: hospital, physician and drug costs, roughly 80-90% of premiums
Administrative costs: claims processing, customer service, IT
Sales and broker commissions: acquiring employer and individual members
Care management: nurse lines, disease management, prior authorization
margins: Insurers typically earn low-to-mid single-digit net margins because the ACA sets minimum medical loss ratios (80% individual/small group, 85% large group); scale, medical cost trend, and Medicare Advantage risk-coding drive the spread.

key_metrics.name: Medical loss ratio (MLR) / medical cost ratio
key_metrics.what: Medical costs as a share of premiums; the core profitability gauge for payers.

key_metrics.name: Members / lives covered
key_metrics.what: Enrollment by segment; drives scale and bargaining power.

key_metrics.name: Per member per month (PMPM)
key_metrics.what: Premium or cost normalized per member; the standard unit for pricing and cost trend.

key_metrics.name: Medical cost trend
key_metrics.what: Annual growth in cost per member; must be priced into premiums.

key_metrics.name: Star ratings
key_metrics.what: CMS quality ratings for Medicare Advantage plans; drive bonus payments and enrollment.

key_metrics.name: Administrative expense ratio
key_metrics.what: Admin costs over revenue; measures operating efficiency.

key_metrics.name: Generic dispensing rate
key_metrics.what: Share of prescriptions filled with generics; a key PBM cost lever.

trends: Elevated medical utilization pressuring Medicare Advantage and commercial margins
Tighter Medicare Advantage payment rates and scrutiny of risk-adjustment coding
Medicaid redeterminations and funding changes shifting enrollment and acuity
PBM reform efforts targeting rebate practices and spread pricing
GLP-1 drug costs straining employer and payer pharmacy budgets
Vertical integration of insurers with PBMs, clinics and home health, under regulatory scrutiny

case_angles.question: A Medicare Advantage insurer's medical costs are rising faster than premiums. What should it do?
Should a regional health insurer enter the ACA individual exchange market in a new state?
How should an insurer respond to employers leaving for a new tech-enabled competitor?
Should a payer acquire a primary care provider group?

interview_hooks: Does vertical integration of payers, PBMs and providers lower costs or entrench market power?
Is Medicare Advantage good value for taxpayers compared with traditional Medicare?
Should PBMs be restructured or have their rebate model banned?
